beats.text: The life cycle begins with a cluster of fertilized frog eggs floating in the water.
These eggs hatch into swimming tadpoles equipped with tails and gills for aquatic life.
As development progresses, the tadpole begins to grow hind legs, starting its physical transformation.
Next, the tadpole grows front limbs and starts resorbing its tail, transitioning into a young froglet.
Finally, the tail disappears completely as it becomes a fully grown adult frog capable of laying eggs, completing the life cycle.

An overarching analytical quality control system oversees the entire refining and separation operation.
A distributed network of sampling points connects directly to this control framework to evaluate material at critical process stages.
The process begins at the feedstock tanks, where raw material and initial flue gases are sampled at point SP1.
Feedstock is pumped forward into a preheating stage, monitored closely by sampling point SP2.
The corresponding high-pressure feedstock pump and preheater unit is introduced into the physical equipment line.
Next in line is the heating furnace block, tracked by another dedicated sampling point SP2.
The physical heating furnace is added, raising the feedstock temperature to vaporization while discharging flue gas.
The vaporized feed enters the distillation column, continuously monitored across sampling points SP3 and SP4.
A physical distillation column and overhead condenser are installed to separate volatile components from heavier fractions.
The process flow adds a condensation and cooling block using circulating cooling water, monitored by points SP5 and SP8.
Finally, purified fractions accumulate in intermediate storage tanks, completing a fully instrumented and quality-controlled distillation workflow.
The process begins with the molecule labeled Phenol, where a hydroxide ion abstracts a proton from the oxygen atom.
This generates a phenoxide intermediate, with electron flow shifting into the ring.
Through resonance, coordination occurs with a sodium cation and carbon dioxide, as the ring attacks the carbon dioxide molecule.
The reaction proceeds to an intermediate where internal electron shifts and proton transfer restore the aromatic ring.
The resulting carboxylate species then accepts a proton from a hydronium ion.
This final protonation yields the target compound, labeled Salicylic acid.
The reaction begins with the divinyl ketone starting material alongside an incoming molecule of ammonia.
Ammonia attacks the terminal alkene carbon, shifting the double bond and pushing electron density onto the carbonyl oxygen.
This conjugate addition generates a zwitterionic enolate intermediate with a positively charged ammonium group and a negatively charged oxygen.
Curved arrows show electron movement as the enolate oxygen abstracts a proton from the ammonium nitrogen.
This proton transfer establishes equilibrium with the neutral enol intermediate bearing a primary amino chain.
Tautomerization of the enol reforms the carbonyl group, orienting the amine toward the remaining double bond.
The primary amine initiates intramolecular conjugate addition, attacking the alkene and pushing electrons onto the carbonyl oxygen.
Cyclization closes the six-membered piperidine core, yielding a cyclic zwitterionic enolate intermediate.
A subsequent proton transfer shifts a proton from the secondary ammonium center to the negatively charged oxygen.
This step forms the neutral cyclic enol intermediate, four-hydroxytetrahydropyridine.
Finally, keto-enol tautomerization converts the cyclic enol into the final four-piperidone product.
This diagram illustrates the overall layout of the AC Refrigerant Cycle.
At the top of the system is the Compressor.
Exiting the compressor, the refrigerant flows as a gas at high pressure and high temperature past a measurement position.
The line feeds into the Condenser, which contains high-pressure saturated vapour, internal coils, and a fan releasing heat outward.
Leaving the condenser, the refrigerant transitions to liquid at high pressure and low temperature, routed past another measurement position.
The line connects to the Expansion Valve positioned at the bottom of the loop.
From the expansion valve, it continues as liquid at low pressure and low temperature past a measurement position.
It flows into the Evaporator on the left, identified with low pressure saturated vapour and an internal fan.
Exiting the evaporator, the refrigerant returns as a gas at low pressure and high temperature through a final measurement position back to the compressor.
The central circular arrows demonstrate the continuous clockwise flow across all four stages of the cycle.

The diagram opens with the Attack Path, highlighted in red along the top.
It begins with a malicious repository, where the attacker controls the source.
This repository contains a poisoned AGENTS.md file, where hidden instructions live in plain sight.
Moving forward, the agent reads it, loading the poisoned file.
The agent trusts it, treating the attacker instructions as valid.
Consequently, the agent sends secrets to the attacker as data exfiltration happens.
Across the central dividing line, the Defense Path is introduced in green.
Here, external input is treated as untrusted by default.
A hook validates the input, scanning for patterns, risks, and injections.
Next, allowlist checks ensure that only approved files and sources pass.
Sandbox limits then restrict available tools, files, network access, and permissions.
Finally, only safe actions run, ensuring the agent cannot hurt what it cannot reach.
At the bottom left, the core attack takeaway states: trust everything equals dangerous.
At the bottom right, the defense takeaway concludes: review config files like code.

items.title: Photon emission in the Bohr atom

beats.text: At the center of the atom sits the dense, positively charged nucleus.
Surrounding the nucleus is the first quantized energy level, designated as n equals one.
A second circular orbit appears further out, corresponding to the principal quantum number n equals two.
The third orbit, n equals three, establishes a higher excited energy level for the electron.
An electron occupies this outer orbit, placing the atom in an excited state.
The electron drops from the third energy level down to the second level via a quantum jump.
This transition releases the excess energy as an emitted photon, illustrating light emission in the Bohr model of the atom.
The legend identifies the particle types: proton, neutron, positron, gamma ray, and neutrino. The circular reaction sequence begins at carbon-12.
A proton labeled 1H interacts with carbon-12, releasing a gamma ray photon and producing nitrogen-13.
Nitrogen-13 decays by releasing a positron and a neutrino, transforming into carbon-13.
A second proton interacts with carbon-13, emitting a gamma ray and forming nitrogen-14.
Another proton joins nitrogen-14, releasing a gamma ray to yield oxygen-15.
Oxygen-15 then decays, releasing a positron and a neutrino to become nitrogen-15.
Finally, a fourth proton interacts with nitrogen-15, releasing helium-4 and regenerating carbon-12 to complete the cycle.

Finally, the path ascends from point four back to point one, completing the closed loop of the cycle.

The process begins with two incoming gluons from colliding protons, initiating gluon-gluon fusion.
Internal top-quark lines mediate the interaction, meeting at a central Yukawa interaction vertex.
A Higgs boson is radiated from the top-quark vertex, propagating outward.
The Higgs boson promptly decays into a bottom and anti-bottom quark pair.
Meanwhile, the accompanying top and anti-top quarks propagate outward in associated production.
Each top quark undergoes weak decay, emitting a charged W-plus and W-minus boson, respectively.
The top decays leave behind energetic bottom and anti-bottom spectator quarks.
The W-plus boson decays hadronically into a quark and anti-quark pair.
The W-minus boson decays leptonically into a charged lepton and an anti-neutrino, completing the semileptonic ttH signature.

A free neutron travels downward to initiate the first generation of nuclear fission.
The incident neutron strikes a fissile uranium-235 nucleus, triggering an unstable state.
The nucleus undergoes fission, splitting into two lighter fission fragments and releasing an energetic burst.
One emitted neutron is captured by a non-fissile uranium-238 nucleus, ending that branch with no further fission.
A second neutron escapes the system entirely without inducing another reaction.
The third neutron strikes another uranium-235 nucleus to carry the reaction into the second generation.
This second uranium-235 nucleus fissions, releasing another burst of energy and two new fragments.
One of the newly released neutrons moves toward a uranium-235 nucleus in the third generation.
That nucleus fissions into fragments and releases three additional neutrons.
Meanwhile, the second neutron from generation two strikes another uranium-235 nucleus in generation three.
It splits into fragments and emits three more neutrons, completing a model of a sustaining uranium-235 fission chain reaction across three generations.

We begin with a clean metal target ready to be illuminated by incident light.
Red light with a wavelength of 700 nanometers hits the surface, but its photon energy is too low to liberate any electrons.
Next, a green photon with a shorter wavelength of 550 nanometers strikes the plate with higher energy.
This photon exceeds the work function, ejecting a photoelectron that escapes at a moderate velocity.
Shorter-wavelength blue light delivers an even greater photon energy of 3.1 electron volts to the surface.
The blue photon ejects an electron with significantly higher speed, demonstrating how photon energy dictates electron kinetic energy in the photoelectric effect.
The legend at the bottom defines the particles: red spheres represent protons, gray spheres represent neutrons, and white spheres represent positrons, alongside symbols for gamma rays and neutrinos.
At the top left, two hydrogen-one protons interact, emitting a positron and a neutrino to produce hydrogen-two, consisting of one proton and one neutron.
Down the left branch, the hydrogen-two nucleus combines with another hydrogen-one proton, emitting a gamma ray and forming helium-three.
In a parallel sequence on the top right, two hydrogen-one protons interact, releasing a positron and a neutrino to yield hydrogen-two.
That hydrogen-two nucleus merges with an incoming hydrogen-one proton, releasing a gamma ray to produce a second helium-three nucleus.
Finally, both helium-three nuclei converge, releasing two hydrogen-one protons and forming a single helium-four nucleus at the bottom.
